items.q: What does `assert add(2, 3) == 5` do when `add` is correct, and when it's broken?
options: If the result equals 5, nothing happens; if it doesn't, it raises AssertionError and stops

explain.right: An assert checks a claim: it's silent when true and raises AssertionError (halting the run) when false.
explain.wrong: It doesn't print, doesn't always error, and can't fix code — it only verifies your stated expectation.

items.q: For pytest to automatically find and run a test, how should it be written?
options: Any function at all is run as a test
As a function whose name starts with `test_`, typically in a file named `test_*.py`, containing asserts
It must print 'PASS' at the end

explain.right: pytest discovers functions named test_... in test_*.py files and treats a passing (non-raising) run as a pass.
explain.wrong: Not every function is a test; the test_ naming convention is how pytest finds them, and no print of 'PASS' is needed.

items.q: Your pytest suite is all green. What does that actually prove?
options: The specific cases you wrote tests for behave as expected — nothing about inputs you didn't test
The program is perfect and bug-free for every possible input
The code will never need changing

explain.right: Green means the behaviours you checked hold; it says nothing about untested inputs, so coverage and honest test choice matter.
explain.wrong: Tests can't prove total correctness or future-proofing, but they're far from useless — they guard the cases you wrote.

items.q: Why should each test set up its own fresh data (e.g. start from an empty list)?
options: So tests don't depend on each other's order or leftovers, keeping each failure meaningful and isolated
To make tests run slower on purpose

explain.right: Independent tests can run in any order and a failure points at one behaviour, not at pollution from a previous test.
explain.wrong: It isn't about slowing tests or a pytest rule; the point is isolation so results are trustworthy.

items.q: In one or two sentences, explain the habit of 'write a failing test for a bug, then fix the code'. Why is it valuable?
rubric: First reproduce the bug as a test that fails, confirming you've captured it
Then change the code until the test passes (goes green)
The test stays in the suite and prevents the bug from silently returning (a regression guard)

explain.right: Good answers capture reproduce-then-fix and note the test becomes a permanent guard against the bug recurring.
explain.wrong: A weak answer just says 'write tests' without the reproduce-first idea or the regression-protection payoff.
